newsitem.title: FINLAND: FINNISH BONDS SEEN UNDERPERFORMING AT YEAR-END.
newsitem.headline: FINNISH BONDS SEEN UNDERPERFORMING AT YEAR-END.

text.p: Finnish bonds may continue to underperform German Bunds as the year-end approaches, defying strong fundamentals, analysts said on Monday.

The 2006 yield gap over Germany started widening three weeks ago amid jitters that followed a rise in German money rates but before that, the yield premium fell eight basis points to 40 in an initial reaction to the linkage to Europe's Exchange Rate Mechanism (ERM) on October 14.
The yield gap is now steadily increasing and some analysts said it could rise as high as 80 basis points from 67 currently.

"There are really two basic reasons, one is that after the ERM link, we were very close to Germany (prompting profit-taking) and the other is the approaching year-end," said Jukka Lepomaki head analyst at Merita Bank.
Particularly domestic investors are already preparing to close their books for the year and the market suffers from a lack of buyers and liquidity, analysts said.
"The spread would be at maximum 50 basis points if the calendar year would not be close to its end," said OKOBANK analyst Teijo Rantatupa.
Foreign investors have also contributed to the widening Finnish/German yield gap by taking profits and unwinding earlier spread trades since the markka's ERM peg, analysts said.
But they also said the current yield premium was too high since Finland ranks among the countries meeting the Maastricht criteria for Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) in 1999.

On the other hand, recent debate on which countries will meet public debt and budget deficit criteria has lead to growing nervousness on whether EMU will be postponed and this has affected peripheral EMU candidates in particular.

"The debate on which countries will be among the first to join has reduced the attractivness of peripheral areas," Lepomaki said, but addded: "If EMU will come true Finland will still be among the first countries to join."

Comments by the Social Democratic Party's newly elected parliamentary group leader Erkki Tuomioja last week that Finland's EMU membership was not desirable in 1999 prompted Danish Unibank to conclude that Finland could still choose to remain outside EMU, even if it met the criteria for joining.
"This could be one of the reasons why Finnish yields have (recently) not tracked the convergence trend," Unibank said in its weekly report.

But analysts said Finnish fundamentals were positive and as long as next year's labour market talks on wages and the framework for accepting EMU and the general political situation do not produce negative surprises, there would be scope for continued convergence in yields next year.
"An attractively wide spread guarantees overseas interest in Finnish bonds," Rantatupa said.
"Investors could consider buying Finnish long bonds against unlikely EMU participants such as for instance Italy," Unibank said.
